items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon takes the MathArena crown but costs 15 times more than GPT-6.1 Sol
items.desc: For the first time in a while, no OpenAI model leads the MathArena AI math benchmark. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and Anthropic's Fable 5.2 have knocked GPT-6.1 Sol from the top, though both cost significantly more. Gemini ignored the time limit in testing and almost never gave up on a task. The article Gemini 4 Carbon takes the MathArena crown but costs 15 times more than GPT-6.1 Sol appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon has become the first non-OpenAI model in a while to top the MathArena math benchmark. It knocked GPT-6.1 Sol from the top spot, while Claude Fable 5.2 came in second, making it potentially one of the most capable publicly available models for math tasks. OpenAI's models, which recently allegedly solved demanding equations like the Navier-Stokes equations , aren't publicly available yet. Gemini 4 Carbon's most common failure mode is exceeding the time limit. The model also almost never gives up on a task, a trait that can be read as either positive or negative . In one case, it launched a script that ran for more than eleven hours without checking on its progress. That extra performance comes at a price, though. With the reasoning settings used in testing, Carbon and Fable 5.2 cost roughly 15 and 40 times as much as GPT-6.1 Sol, respectively. items.title: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
items.desc: OpenAI is dissolving its standalone robotics team for the second time, but not because it lacks data. General-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can apparently control robots directly, making a dedicated unit unnecessary. The researchers are being redistributed across other teams in what the company frames as a way to accelerate its robotics efforts. The article OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI is apparently disbanding its robotics team again, but this time for different reasons than in 2020. Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization. OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, which then sat empty, Fortune reports . OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly , reducing the need for specialized robotics models. Ad In an Nvidia study , an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one. Ad A new robotics benchmark called StationeryBench compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, Astra running on a humanoid robot navigated and cleaned up a kitchen. It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from Anthropic and Google have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in cost and reliability as well as speed and energy consumption , even if they don't generalize as well. Ad Yoav Artzi , an AI researcher at Cornell University and Google DeepMind, also sees Astra as a major leap in spatial understanding . On the still-unpublished REMAP benchmark, GPT-6 Astra reaches near-human accuracy, according to Artzi. He suspects that OpenAI may have trained the model on large amounts of 3D training data such as Blender scenes. OpenAI shut down its robotics division in 2020 because, according to co-founder Wojciech Zaremba, the company lacked the training data it needed and large language models were a faster path to AGI. The company rebuilt the team in 2024. CEO Sam Altman is reportedly targeting a first public robot demo for 2027 , and OpenAI wants to build its own everyday robots in the long term. But the company also faces heavy financial pressure to focus on its core AI business , where it has lost significant ground to Anthropic . items.title: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon
items.desc: Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon points to a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow as a reason he left, saying it shows the company's algorithms are improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate. Coxon continues to call for a pause on frontier model development so competitors can catch up and human-level AI can become a commodity. The article Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Jacob Coxon, former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher who brought AI fears into the mainstream, says a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow was a major reason he quit. Coxon says a slide Anthropic released for its IPO roadshow was a key reason he left the company after only about four months. The chart shows how much compute Anthropic needs over time to train its models, and the axis is compressed so that a 10x and a 100x increase barely look different. Yet the curve still climbs steeply, which Coxon says shows that algorithmic efficiency is improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate. "It's an insane plot and I'm surprised they made it public," he writes. Ad Coxon argues that Anthropic's Mythos model, a major capability jump in the spring, was part of this accelerating trend. "Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed," he writes. Ad He says algorithmic improvements are "on the verge of being automated," which is why he wants frontier model development paused next year so competitors can catch up. A pause, he writes, would "commoditize human-level intelligence. It would only harm OpenAI and Anthropic." Coxon previously trained AI models at OpenAI and, most recently, Anthropic. He drew wide attention in September with public warnings about the risks of advanced AI systems , echoed by other protagonists in the industry. One of their fears is that advanced, self-improving AI could get out of control. items.title: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
items.desc: Runway releases its robotics model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code under the Apache 2.0 license. The model uses knowledge from video training for robot control and leads the World Action Model category on Nvidia's RoboLab-120 benchmark. It can't yet plan complex action sequences on its own, though. The article Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI company Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code. The model uses what it learned from video to control robots and shows promising results in the company's own tests. Runway has released Praxis-1, its AI model for controlling robots. The company first introduced Praxis-1 in late September but initially gave access only to select partners. Alongside the release, Runway published a detailed research report with new performance tests. Runway's model weights and source code are available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use. Ad Praxis-1 takes in camera images, text instructions, and information about a robot's position. From those inputs, it predicts how the environment will change and calculates the right robot movements. As new camera frames come in, the model continuously adjusts its control. Ad Praxis-1 builds on a video model that learned how objects move and interact from ordinary footage. Runway then fine-tuned it with videos of human actions and robot data. This approach could reduce the need for expensive robot-specific datasets, which have traditionally been collected just to train these kinds of systems. Runway is best known for generative video models like Gen-4.5 . With Praxis-1, the company is bringing its video research into robotics. Runway calls Praxis-1 a World Action Model that predicts how a scene will change and derives matching robot movements from those predictions. Since September, robotics companies Standard Bots, Noble Machines, and Ultra have been testing Praxis-1 on different systems, including a humanoid robot, an industrial robot arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot. Ad Praxis-1 still needs some specialized robot data. To adapt it to a Franka robot arm, Runway used about 277 hours of recordings from the public DROID research dataset, according to its research report . Those recordings show robots grasping and moving objects, for example. For a dual-arm robot, the company used between 1,400 and 2,600 hours of training material. Runway had already used DROID data and data from other robot systems during earlier training stages. Whether the approach actually needs less robot data overall than comparable models without general video pretraining is still an open question. On Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard , Praxis-1 scores a 46.2 percent success rate. The benchmark tests how reliably robot models can sort, grasp, or stack objects across 120 tasks in simulation. FLUX 3 Action , also built as a World Action Model, scores 42.9 percent under the same test conditions. That puts Praxis-1 at the top of the World Action Model category. In the overall leaderboard, it ranks fifth behind two AI agents and two robot models with different architectures. Runway ran all the tests itself, and the results haven't been independently verified yet. Ad After fine-tuning on DROID data, Runway tested the model on a real Franka robot arm. Both models had to complete the same ten tasks, like placing a banana on a plate or closing a drawer. With ten attempts per task, Praxis-1 succeeded 88 times, while FLUX 3 Action managed 80. items.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
items.desc: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.title: Firm linked to Jensen Huang's ex-lover reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for China
items.desc: Megaspeed, the firm owned by ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's former lover Alice Huang, arranged nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for Chinese companies between 2024 and 2025, according to the WSJ. Short seller Culper Research estimates Nvidia's actual China revenue share exceeds 20 percent, far above the officially reported 7 percent. The article Firm linked to Jensen Huang's ex-lover reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for China appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Megaspeed arranged nearly $12 billion worth of Nvidia high-performance chip orders for Chinese companies between March 2024 and June 2025, according to documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal. The company is owned by Alice Huang, the former lover of since-ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Megaspeed shipped the chips to buyers in China who maintained long-standing business ties with local tech giants, the WSJ reports. The orders covered several hundred thousand chips that the US had sought to keep out of China through export controls. Megaspeed reportedly gained preferential access to scarce AI chips as an Nvidia cloud partner, apparently because it counted Chinese cloud and tech company Alibaba as a major client. Nvidia officially reported $12.4 billion in China revenue over six months, accounting for 7 percent of total revenue. Short-selling firm Culper Research estimates, however, that more than 20 percent of Nvidia's revenue in the last fiscal year came from Chinese customers. A significant share of that China business may have flowed through indirect channels. items.title: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
items.desc: Australia's central bank sees early signs that AI is hitting young entry-level workers in highly exposed jobs like software development and customer service. Since ChatGPT launched, job postings and employment among 15- to 24-year-olds in those fields have dropped more sharply than among older workers. Author Mike Major cautions against jumping to conclusions, however, noting that business cycle shifts and remote work trends could also explain the numbers. The article Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service appeared first on Th
items.full: AI has barely displaced any jobs in Australia so far, but young workers entering highly exposed fields like software development are faring worse. An analysis by Mike Major for Australia's central bank (RBA) built a monitoring system that focuses on the areas where effects are likely to appear first, namely entry-level workers and highly AI-exposed occupations such as programming , clerical work, and customer service. According to the analysis , job postings have fallen across all groups since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, with the steepest drop in the highest-exposure group. In that group, workers aged 15 to 24 and young college graduates have weaker employment rates and higher unemployment than older workers. Ad Major cautions against drawing early conclusions, since the study does not establish direct causation and measures only theoretical exposure, not actual use by companies. Post-pandemic shifts in the business cycle or in remote work could also be driving the numbers. According to SEEK data, AI is complementing existing work while also creating new demand for AI skills . Ad An August 2025 Stanford study based on millions of US payroll records found a similar pattern, with employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations down 13 percent in relative terms since late 2022 and nearly 20 percent among young software developers. More experienced workers in the same occupations held steady or gained ground. A March 2026 Anthropic study also found signs of declining hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed occupations, with job-finding rates down about 14 percent. It found no systematic rise in overall unemployment, however. Theoretical automation potential and actual AI use are far apart, according to the study. Ad Anthropic offers a company-level example. According to an internal review , the share of junior hires in technical roles has fallen from 27 percent to 9 percent since early 2025. In August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as human employees. Anthropic concedes that, as an extremely AI-intensive software company, it is a special case. Even so, researchers warn of a "tragedy of the cognitive commons" , in which disappearing junior roles lead to a future shortage of experienced professionals, assuming those professionals are still needed. A large study of 25,000 workers in Denmark confirms the lack of economy-wide impact. Despite a 64 percent AI adoption rate, researchers found no measurable changes in wages or hours worked. Workers saved an average of just 2.8 percent of their working time. Ad A January 2026 analysis of 10.6 million LinkedIn profiles and US unemployment data , however, cautions against blaming the downturn on AI alone. The research team led by Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh found that the problems in exposed occupations started in early 2022, months before ChatGPT launched. Macroeconomic factors like the Fed's shift in interest rate policy or a correction after pandemic-era hiring surges may play a bigger role than previously assumed.
